Radar cross section (RCS) measures the detectability of an object by radar, depending on frequency, aspect angle, polarization, and target properties.
PEMC is characterized by a scalar admittance parameter M, with PEC and PMC as limiting cases (M → ±∞ and M=0 respectively).
The study uses duality transformations by Lindell and Sihvola to relate PEC scattering solutions to PEMC scattering.
Soil models used include San Antonio clay loam with 5%, 10%, and 20% water content representing increasing loss factors.
Increasing soil moisture increases electrical conductivity and dielectric loss, attenuating scattered fields and reducing RCS amplitude.
The scattering width of a PEMC strip is affected by the admittance parameter M, with cross-polarized scattering maximal near M=±1.
Co-polarized scattered fields vanish in the PEC and PMC limits, while cross-polarized fields appear in intermediate PEMC cases.
Physical optics approximates induced surface currents on the strip to calculate scattered fields.
Geometrical optics is used to determine reflection coefficients on the strip surface.
The RCS of a finite-width strip differs from an infinite strip due to edge diffraction and different reflection and scattering angles.
Numerical results were generated using Mathematica software to reproduce and extend previous PEMC scattering analyses.
The paper confirms that PEMC media behave as perfect reflectors but differ from PEC and PMC by allowing cross-polarized scattering.
Radar cross section is critical for ground penetrating radar applications to detect subsurface cavities and buried objects.
The scattered field amplitude and RCS decrease as the soil's conductivity and permittivity increase.
The interference nulls in the RCS pattern disappear in lossy media due to attenuation of diffracted energy from strip edges.
The duality transformation relates scattered fields from PEC strips to those from PEMC strips via a linear combination involving M.
The relative permittivity of soil is complex and frequency-dependent, impacting wave propagation and scattering.
The study provides analytical expressions for scattered fields and RCS in terms of strip width, wave number, and soil parameters.
Cross-polarized scattered fields introduce nonreciprocal effects in PEMC scattering not present in PEC or PMC cases.
The paper extends prior work on electromagnetic scattering in lossy media by applying PEMC theory to practical soil models.
